blocks.text: **Vertical scaling** means buying a bigger machine — more CPU, RAM, faster disks. It's the simplest option and goes surprisingly far (a single server with 100+ cores and terabytes of RAM exists), but it has a ceiling, gets disproportionately expensive near the top, and leaves you with a single point of failure.

**Horizontal scaling** means adding more machines and spreading work across them. It's how internet-scale systems grow, but it only works cleanly for **stateless** components. The design move that makes it possible is pushing state out of the app tier into databases, caches and object stores.

items: Sessions in a shared store (Redis) or a signed token (JWT) instead of server memory.
Uploaded files to object storage, not the local disk.
Caches either shared (Redis) or treated as disposable per-instance.
Any instance can serve any request → instances can be added, removed or replaced at will.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Once the app tier is stateless, scaling it is an autoscaling-group problem. The hard scaling problems move to the stateful tiers: the database, caches and queues.

sections.title: What a load balancer actually does

items: Distributes requests across healthy instances and removes unhealthy ones via **health checks** (active probes and passive error tracking).
Terminates TLS so backends don't have to.
Connection draining: on deploy, stop sending new requests to an instance but let in-flight ones finish.
Is itself redundant (active–active pairs, or a managed cloud LB).

How it chooses
Best for

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: "Power of two random choices" is a great interview detail: it avoids the herd behaviour of always picking the global minimum, needs no global state, and gets exponentially better load balance than pure random.

sections.title: Sticky sessions — and why to avoid them

blocks.text: Sticky sessions pin a user to one backend (via a cookie or IP hash) so in-memory session state works. They break even load distribution, lose sessions when the instance dies, and complicate deploys. Prefer stateless instances; use stickiness only for genuinely stateful connections (WebSocket gateways), and even then design for reconnection to another node.

items: Scale on a metric that tracks load: CPU, requests per instance, queue depth, or p95 latency.
Scale out fast, scale in slowly (cooldowns) to avoid flapping.
Pre-warm or schedule capacity for known spikes — autoscaling reacts in minutes, a flash crowd arrives in seconds.
Keep startup fast (small images, lazy initialisation) so new instances help quickly.

cols.title: Active–passive
cons: Failover takes minutes; standby capacity is idle

cols.title: Active–active
pros: Low latency everywhere; survives region loss
cons: Data conflicts across regions; harder consistency

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd scale the stateless tier horizontally behind an L7 load balancer with health checks and least-request routing, and keep state in a replicated database and shared cache.
